header:
Date: 2027-08-09
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Recording: yes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Evan Brooks (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Opal CTO), Sofia Morales (Opal ML Lead), Liam O'Connor (Opal Infra)
summary: Discovery focused on model selection for Opal's multilingual customer support agent. Key themes: 8k vs 32k context, hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) tradeoffs, tool-calling support for internal APIs, SOC2/KMS requirements, benchmark plan and next steps for trial.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private deployment tradeoffs
transcript:
[00:00] Evan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Evan Brooks from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Maya our solutions engineer. Quick intros?
[00:10] Ravi: Hi, I'm Ravi, CTO at Opal. We build the customer support automation platform.
[00:16] Sofia: Sofia, ML lead, focusing on multilingual NLU and dialog.
[00:20] Liam: Liam, infra, I handle cloud networking and security.
[00:24] Maya: Great, thanks. Goal for today is kickoff model selection discussion - open models, context length, multilingual and tool-calling. We'll ask a few questions about production constraints.
[00:34] Ravi: Sounds good. Quick context - we've piloted with a hosted API from another provider but running into cost and latency at scale, also worried about data residency. Looking at Redwood for either hosted or dedicated/reserved, maybe private later.
[00:48] Maya: Got it. Can you share your workload? Is it live chat, async support threads, long context retrieval?
[00:55] Sofia: It's a mix. Primary use case is triaging long support threads - sometimes 8-12k tokens, and for escalations we want up to 30k context (customer history + docs). Also low-latency for suggested replies (under 400ms ideally) for agent assist. Multilingual: EN/ES/FR/JPN but mostly EN + ES.
[01:20] Evan: Good - that maps to the 8k vs 32k question. For 30k workloads, we'll look at models that support 32k context windows or chaining strategies with retrieval and KV cache. Do you need true 32k for end-to-end reasoning or is summarization acceptable?
[01:38] Sofia: For some cases we need full thread context, especially in legal/regulatory tickets where details matter. Summaries sometimes miss nuance.
[01:46] Maya: Understood. Two options: 1) use a native 32k model (we have verified open variants with 32k contexts) or 2) use 8k models with retrieval + prefix KV cache or chunking plus deterministic summarization. Tradeoffs are latency and cost.
[02:05] [cross-talk] Ravi: Latency is big for the agent assist path. If agent expects suggestions in sub-500ms, bigger contexts will add cost.
[02:14] Maya: Right. For hosted we can route low-latency traffic to smaller specialized models and escalate to higher-context on-demand. For Dedicated, you get predictable throughput and lower per-token cost for sustained volume - also data stays in dedicated GPUs.
[02:30] Liam: For private, we need VPC peering and customer-managed KMS. Any handwritten docs?
[02:36] Evan: Yes we'll send our security whitepaper. We support VPC peering and bring-your-own-KMS / HSM for Private. For Dedicated we can integrate with your KMS too, but Private gives you the control plane on your side.
[02:51] Sofia: How do the open models compare on multilingual capability? We've seen big drift in Spanish slang.
[02:58] Maya: Good question. Some open models pretrained on multilingual corpora perform well, but fine-tuning or instruction tuning with your language samples helps. We recommend evaluation sets per language. We can run evals across candidate open models (e.g., Llama variants, Mistral open, Falcon derivatives) and show Rouge/Exact-Match and qualitative examples.
[03:20] Evan: Competitors folks often push proprietary models; we focus on curated open models + Redwood-verified performance so you can pick the correct latency/cost point.
[03:30] Ravi: On tool-calling - we need deterministic function calls to internal APIs for order lookups, ticket updates, and secure redaction of PII. Any built-in tooling?
[03:40] Maya: We support structured tool-calling: function signatures, typed inputs/outputs and guaranteed fallback policies. There's also an option to run tools in customer environment via secure connectors for sensitive calls.
[03:51] Sofia: So if the model tries to call a tool, we need 1) authentication and 2) strict allowlist - can Redwood do that?
[03:57] Evan: Yes. You can register tools and set per-tool RBAC. For Private deployments, the tool endpoints never transit Redwood control plane if you prefer.
[04:07] Liam: For compliance we need audit logs for every tool call and model input/output retention rules. What's retention look like?
[04:15] Maya: We emit per-request audit logs and you can configure retention. For Dedicated and Private, logs can be pushed to your S3 or SIEM. Hosted can keep logs for X days by default but enterprise plans allow custom retention. We'll share specifics.
[04:30] Ravi: Back to models: can you run benchmarks with both 8k and 32k contexts? We want token-level cost estimates and latency percentiles at our expected QPS.
[04:40] Maya: Yes - we'll run a benchmark using your prompt set and sample traffic. We'll include tail latency (p95/p99), CPU/GPU utilization estimates, and suggested batching configs. For Dedicated we can project committed capacity and expected unit costs.
[04:53] Sofia: Any notes on quantization - we care about quality. Some quantized variants reduce cost but change behavior.
[04:59] Maya: Exactly. We can test int8/int4 quantized variants; our Optimize toolkit recommends quantization profiles per workload and flags regressions. For sensitive production flows we recommend gating quantized models behind evals first.
[05:14] [00:05:14] Ravi: Are there size/perf tradeoffs between Mistral / Llama / Falcon families?
[05:20] Maya: Generally, Mistral-style models punch above weight on some tasks; Llama-family has strong open ecosystem and tooling; Falcon variants historically had strong English performance. The right pick depends on your evals (multilingual, instruction-following, code/tool-call reliability). We'll surface per-model metrics.
[05:39] Sofia: For tool-calling we need deterministic schema outputs - sometimes models hallucinate key names. How do you enforce?
[05:45] Maya: Two levers: strict function signatures (model must return JSON matching schema or call fails) and post-processing validators. Also you can enable automatic fallback to safe-mode where model generates plain text and our agent parses. But strict schemas + a small verification layer reduces hallucination risk.
[06:04] Liam: Network/egress question: if we use Hosted, will data flow through Redwood regions? We have to keep PII in EU.
[06:11] Evan: We have region routing and data residency controls. Hosted in EU region will keep data in EU. Dedicated/Private are preferable for strict residency and isolation. We'll send the region map and compliance notes.
[06:25] [00:06:25] Ravi: Cost - what's the ballpark difference hosted vs dedicated per token?
[06:30] Evan: Hosted is pay-as-you-go and easier to start; Dedicated sees discounts on committed volumes, often 20-40% lower per-token depending on commitment and model/quantization. Private has higher upfront but lower marginal costs for steady state. We'll provide a modeled example for your expected monthly tokens.
[06:49] Sofia: SLA and latency SLO on Dedicated?
[06:53] Maya: We offer SLA-backed uptime and latency targets for Dedicated with predictable capacity and burst options. For true low-latency use we can reserve GPUs in a hot pool.
[07:05] Ravi: For trial we'd like to see 2 things: 1) a hosted POC with our sample prompts, 2) a small dedicated benchmark for sustained load.
[07:14] Evan: Makes sense - typical path is hosted POC to validate quality, then Dedicated pilot for throughput and economics. If you need Private, we can parallelize the security review.
[07:25] [00:07:25] Sofia: On multilingual evaluation - can Redwood score per-language quality and provide confusion matrices?
[07:31] Maya: Yes, our eval harness supports per-language metrics, token-level attention breakdowns, and human-in-the-loop review exports. We'll run EN/ES/FR and surface where models diverge.
[07:44] Liam: Integration surface - do you provide SDKs? We use Python and Node.
[07:49] Evan: Yes, SDKs for Python, Node, and REST. We'll share code samples for streaming responses and function-calling.
[07:58] Ravi: How customizable are model rollouts? We want canary small percent traffic to new model versions.
[08:04] Maya: Rollouts are first-class - canary, A/B, automatic rollback based on quality/regression alerts tied to your eval sets. You can route by route or by customer.
[08:14] Sofia: A few edge questions: 1) do you support mixed-model routing (e.g., short prompts to faster cheaper model, long contexts to high-capacity model)? 2) can we pin model versions per route?
[08:24] Maya: Yes to both. Smart routing supports policy-based dispatch (latency, cost, region) and version pinning per-route.
[08:31] [00:08:31] Ravi: Question on storage of KV cache - is that on the GPU host or external store?
[08:37] Maya: We keep hot KV cache in memory on the serving node for speed; we also snapshot to object store for warm-starts. For Dedicated/Private you can control where snapshots land.
[08:47] Liam: For our security team, we need to see SAML/SSO, RBAC, and audit examples.
[08:53] Evan: We'll attach SSO/SAML docs and RBAC guide. For audit logs we can forward events to your SIEM.
[09:00] Sofia: Can we test function-calls against our staging env with tokens that expire?
[09:05] Maya: Yes - we recommend ephemeral credentials and connector proxies so calls are proxied into your VPC; for hosted the payloads can be proxied through Redwood or via Private connectors.
[09:15] [00:09:15] Ravi: Any known caveats with 32k models on quantization? We saw some hallucination after int8 in another vendor.
[09:23] Maya: Quantization interacts with attention kernels; for some architectures you see quality drop at aggressive quantization. We'll include regression checks in the benchmark. For safety-critical flows keep a non-quantized gold path.
[09:39] Sofia: Examples of open models you recommend testing first?
[09:44] Maya: Llama-3 derivatives, Mistral-instruct variants, and a few Falcon forks; we usually shortlist 3-4 and then run your eval.
[09:52] Evan: We'll prepare a shortlist and recommended starting configs (batching, quantization, KV settings).
[09:58] Liam: For Dedicated capacity, what's lead time to provision GPUs?
[10:03] Evan: Typically 2-4 weeks for standard configs, faster for hosted. Private on-prem is longer and depends on network setup.
[10:11] [00:10:11] Ravi: On pricing, we'll need a model for 1M tokens/month and 10M tokens/month.
[10:17] Evan: We'll include both in the pricing sheet. Also show sensitivity to quantization and batching.
[10:24] Sofia: For tool-calling, when model calls internal API that returns PII, is Redwood able to redact before storing logs?
[10:31] Maya: Yes - we support field-level redaction rules and can avoid logging sensitive fields. For Private, logs can be kept only in your S3 and Redwood never sees them.
[10:43] Ravi: Next steps?
[10:45] Evan: Action items: we'll run a hosted POC with your prompts, run bench on 8k & 32k candidates, send pricing and security docs. Maya will prepare latency/cost estimates.
[10:56] Sofia: We'll send the prompt set by Friday and outline tool endpoints.
[11:01] Liam: I'll follow up on network constraints and KMS requirements.
[11:06] Evan: Great. Recap - hosted POC -> dedicated pilot -> optional private. Benchmarks will decide the final model (likely one of the shortlisted open variants).
[11:16] Ravi: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[11:20] Evan: Thanks - we'll circle back with materials and a follow-up meeting.
[11:25] [END]
